chunks.text: Summary: This guidance updates the World Allergy Organization's 2011 anaphylaxis guidelines, incorporating current knowledge on diagnosis and management. It covers anaphylaxis definition, epidemiology, elicitors, cofactors, severity grading, acute and long-term management, and global availability of epinephrine auto-injectors. The document is intended for healthcare professionals globally, especially in regions without national guidelines.

chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Anaphylaxis
  Synonyms:
    - acute systemic allergic reaction
    - anaphylactic reaction
    - anaphylactic shock
  Description: A serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis involves life-threatening compromise of the airway, breathing, or circulation, and can occur without typical skin features or circulatory shock.
  Epidemiology: Global incidence is estimated at 50–112 episodes per 100,000 person-years, with a lifetime prevalence of 0.3–5.1%. Pediatric incidence ranges widely, from 1 to 761 per 100,000 person-years. Recurrence rates are 26.5–54% over 1.5–25 years. Mortality remains low: drug-induced anaphylaxis 0.05–0.51 per million people/year, food-induced 0.03–0.32, venom-induced 0.09–0.13.
  Clinical presentation: Acute onset (minutes to several hours) of skin/mucosal involvement (generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema of lips, tongue, uvula) plus at least one of: respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia), cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, syncope, collapse), or severe gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting). Alternatively, acute hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after allergen exposure, even without skin signs. Skin involvement is absent in 10–20% of episodes.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Food-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Commonly presents with severe gastrointestinal symptoms; triggered by ingestion of allergenic foods such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, egg, seafood.
    - Name: Venom-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by insect stings (bees, wasps, fire ants); typical systemic reaction with rapid onset.
    - Name: Drug-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Occurs after administration of medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, biologics, chemotherapeutics, contrast media); may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated.
    - Name: Idiopathic anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: No identifiable trigger; accounts for 6.5-35% of cases; requires evaluation for mast cell disorders (mastocytosis, KIT mutation).
    - Name: Alpha-gal-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Delayed onset (hours after ingestion of mammalian meat); associated with IgE to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose.
    - Name: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by physical activity, often with cofactors like food ingestion; may involve specific foods (omega-5-gliadin).
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Serum tryptase (acute)
      Purpose: Confirm mast cell activation during an acute episode
      When indicated: During acute anaphylaxis (within 15 min to 3 h, peak at 1–2 h)
      Interpretation: Elevated levels support anaphylaxis; normal levels do not exclude it. A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used.
    - Test: Serum tryptase (baseline)
      Purpose: Establish individual baseline and detect underlying mast cell disorders
      When indicated: At least 24 h after resolution of symptoms
      Interpretation: Persistently elevated baseline tryptase suggests mastocytosis or clonal mast cell disease.
    - Test: Clinical history and physical examination
      Purpose: Identify potential triggers, cofactors, and risk factors
      When indicated: After acute episode, during specialist assessment
    - Test: Allergen-specific IgE testing and/or skin prick tests
      Purpose: Confirm sensitization to suspected allergens
      When indicated: During specialist allergy workup
    - Test: KIT D816V mutation analysis
      Purpose: Rule out clonal mast cell disorder
      When indicated: In idiopathic anaphylaxis or when baseline tryptase is elevated
      Interpretation: Detection indicates a clonal mast cell disorder (e.g., mastocytosis).
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Serum tryptase (mature β-tryptase)
      Expected result: Elevated (>11.4 mg/L) or significant rise over baseline per consensus equation
      Clinical significance: Indicates mast cell degranulation; supports diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
    - Marker: Baseline serum tryptase
      Expected result: Normal in most individuals; elevated in mastocytosis
      Clinical significance: Elevated baseline increases risk of severe anaphylaxis and suggests need for mast cell workup.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: KIT D816V mutation
      Technique: PCR from peripheral blood or bone marrow
      Clinical significance: Identifies clonal mast cell disorder; indicated in idiopathic anaphylaxis or elevated baseline tryptase.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Observe for at least 6–12 hours after reaction, especially if severe or requiring multiple epinephrine doses. Specialist follow-up for trigger identification and education.
    Recommended tests:
      - Allergen-specific IgE testing
      - Skin prick testing
      - Baseline serum tryptase
      - KIT mutation analysis if indicated
      - Periodic reassessment of comorbidities
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of recurrence
      - Potential for biphasic reactions
      - Psychological impact
      - Need for allergen avoidance or immunotherapy
    Survivorship notes: Patients should carry an epinephrine auto-injector, have a written emergency action plan, wear medical identification, and receive ongoing education on anaphylaxis management.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.
    - Timepoint: After initial treatment and stabilization
      Method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.
  Supportive care:
    - High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
    - Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
    - Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
    - Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
    - Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
  Special considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_02
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: maintenance
  Patient population: Patients who have experienced anaphylaxis, to prevent recurrences.
  Decision rules:
    - Identify trigger(s) through detailed history and confirmatory tests (in vivo and in vitro).
    - Refer to allergist-immunologist for specialized evaluation.
    - Provide written personalized anaphylaxis emergency action plan; teach patient/caregiver to recognize symptoms and administer epinephrine promptly.
    - Prescribe epinephrine auto-injector (or alternative prefilled syringe if auto-injector unavailable); ensure patient/caregiver demonstrates correct technique.
    - Manage risk factors for fatality: optimize asthma control, address cardiovascular diseases, counsel against risk-taking behaviors, educate on seriousness of anaphylaxis.
    - Recommend always carrying a mobile phone, especially for exercise-induced anaphylaxis.
    - Implement measures to avoid triggers: allergen avoidance, allergen immunotherapy (e.g., venom immunotherapy for venom anaphylaxis), drug desensitization when appropriate.
    - Use medical identification (bracelet/wallet card) indicating allergy.
    - Document suspected trigger in medical record (electronic/paper).
    - Provide anaphylaxis education and training to patient, family, and caregivers.
    - Advocate for public health measures (e.g., improved food labelling).
    - Schedule follow-up to reassess original cause and management plan.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Epinephrine auto-injector (or prefilled epinephrine syringe)
      Summary: Carry one or more epinephrine auto-injectors for prompt self-administration in case of recurrence. Inject intramuscularly into antero-lateral thigh, hold for 3-10 seconds, then seek emergency medical help.
      Duration cycles: As needed for future reactions; replace before expiration.
    - Name: Allergen immunotherapy (e.g., venom immunotherapy)
      Summary: For venom-induced anaphylaxis, allergen immunotherapy is indicated to reduce risk of future systemic reactions.
      Duration cycles: Typically 3-5 years, as per guidelines.
    - Name: Drug desensitization
      Summary: For drug hypersensitivity when the drug is essential and no alternatives exist.
      Duration cycles: Temporary desensitization; repeated for each treatment course.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: At follow-up visits
      Method: Review of any subsequent allergic reactions, adherence to avoidance measures, and proper use of epinephrine auto-injector technique.
      Interpretation: Reassess trigger identification, need for continued immunotherapy, and update action plan.
  Supportive care:
    - Anaphylaxis education: train patient and caregivers to recognize early signs and promptly use epinephrine.
    - Written personalized anaphylaxis emergency action plan.
    - Medical identification bracelet/wallet card.
    - Advice to carry mobile phone.
    - Management of comorbidities (asthma, cardiovascular disease).
    - Public health advocacy for allergen labelling.
  Special considerations: In regions where epinephrine auto-injectors are unavailable or unaffordable, provide alternative such as prefilled epinephrine syringes or vials, with training on proper injection technique. For patients with exercise-induced anaphylaxis, emphasize carrying mobile phone and avoiding exercise alone.

chunks.text:
Therapies index:
  Name: Epinephrine (adrenaline)
  Type: drug
  Approved indications:
    - First-line treatment for anaphylaxis
  Administration: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis of the quadriceps (antero-lateral thigh) at a dose of 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.5 mg), repeated every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. For self-administration, auto-injectors, prefilled syringes, or ampoule with syringe may be used. In healthcare settings, intravenous infusion (low-dose) via pump may be used for refractory reactions. Nebulized epinephrine may be considered for upper airway obstruction.
  Key toxicities:
    - Generally well-tolerated when administered intramuscularly
    - Intravenous bolus can cause potentially fatal arrhythmias
  Monitoring:
    - Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status

chunks.text:
Toxicities:
  - Event: Cardiac arrhythmias (potentially fatal)
    Associated therapies:
    - epinephrine (intravenous bolus)
    Management:
    - Severity: any
    Actions: Intravenous epinephrine should be avoided for initial anaphylaxis treatment; if administered, it must be given as an intravenous infusion via pump with cardiac monitoring, and only by personnel experienced in diluting and administering the correct doses.
    Prevention:
    - Use intramuscular epinephrine as first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
  - Event: Hypotension
    Associated therapies:
    - chlorpheniramine (intravenous)
    Management:
    - Severity: any
    Actions: Avoid rapid intravenous administration of first-generation H1-antihistamines; consider using second-generation antihistamines to minimize adverse effects.
    Prevention:
    - Administer antihistamines cautiously; prefer second-generation agents when available.
  - Event: Sedation
    Associated therapies:
    - H1-antihistamines (first-generation)
    Management:
    - Severity: any
    Actions: Substitute with second-generation antihistamines to reduce sedative effects.
    Prevention:
    - Use second-generation antihistamines in preference to first-generation agents.
  - Event: Biphasic anaphylactic reaction
    Incidence: Approximately 50% occur within the first 6–12 hours after the initial reaction.
    Recognition:
    - Return of anaphylaxis symptoms after apparent resolution of the initial episode.
    Management:
    - Severity: all
    Actions: Observe patients in a healthcare setting, especially those with severe initial reactions or those requiring multiple doses of epinephrine; extended observation may be warranted.

chunks.text:
Recommendations:
  - Rec id: rec_01
    Statement: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
    Source heading: ABSTRACT
  - Rec id: rec_02
    Statement: All anaphylaxis reactions must be treated with intramuscular adrenaline to reduce the risk of death.
    Context: Emphasized despite most anaphylaxis reactions not being immediately life-threatening.
    Rationale: Fatal outcomes are rare, but unpredictability of progression necessitates treatment.
    Source heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_03
    Statement: Early suspicion of anaphylaxis, based on symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, should prompt immediate management.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_04
    Statement: Initial management of anaphylaxis includes removing the trigger if possible, assessing airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin, calling emergency services, injecting intramuscular epinephrine, and positioning the patient.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_05
    Statement: Intramuscular epinephrine should be injected into the antero-lateral thigh (vastus lateralis muscle).
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_06
    Statement: The recommended epinephrine dose for healthcare professionals is 0.01 mg/kg body weight, up to a maximum total dose of 0.5 mg, administered intramuscularly.
    Context: Simplified dosing table provided: infants under 10 kg: 0.01 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL; children 1–5 years: 0.15 mg; children 6–12 years: 0.3 mg; teenagers and adults: 0.5 mg.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_07
    Statement: Epinephrine dosing may be repeated every 5–15 minutes if symptoms are refractory to initial treatment.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_08
    Statement: Intravenous epinephrine is not recommended for initial treatment of anaphylaxis due to the risk of fatal arrhythmias from bolus administration.
    Rationale: Intravenous bolus epinephrine can cause fatal arrhythmias.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_09
    Statement: If intravenous epinephrine is used, it should be administered as a continuous infusion via an infusion pump in monitored patients by experienced personnel.
    Context: Low-dose epinephrine infusion protocols exist and have demonstrated safety and efficacy.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_10
    Statement: For upper airway obstruction, consider adding nebulized epinephrine.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_11
    Statement: High-flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) should be administered to all patients with respiratory distress and those receiving repeated doses of epinephrine.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_12
    Statement: Intravenous access should be established using large-bore cannulae (14 or 16 gauge for adults).
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_13
    Statement: Intravenous crystalloid fluid boluses (20 mL/kg) should be given to patients with cardiovascular instability.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_14
    Statement: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous chest compressions should be performed when indicated.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_15
    Statement: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol) may be used for bronchoconstriction, but are not a substitute for repeated intramuscular epinephrine if symptoms persist.
    Rationale: Bronchodilators do not replace the need for epinephrine.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_16
    Statement: Frequent and regular monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status is recommended.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_17
    Statement: H1-antihistamines have a limited role in anaphylaxis treatment but may help relieve cutaneous symptoms; their administration should not delay epinephrine injection.
    Context: Second-generation antihistamines are preferred if available, but first-generation ones are the only parenteral options. Some guidelines now consider antihistamines a third-line treatment.
    Rationale: Antihistamine use can delay more urgent epinephrine administration.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_18
    Statement: Routine use of glucocorticosteroids in acute anaphylaxis is controversial and may not be beneficial; their administration is not essential.
    Context: They are commonly used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, but evidence of benefit is lacking and they may cause harm.
    Rationale: Increasing evidence shows no benefit and potential harm.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_19
    Statement: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis refractory to epinephrine, particularly those taking beta-blockers.
    Context: Evidence is very limited.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_20
    Statement: Patients with anaphylaxis should be observed, especially those with severe reactions or requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
    Context: About half of biphasic reactions occur within 6–12 hours.
    Rationale: Biphasic reactions can occur, necessitating observation.
    Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_21
    Statement: Baseline serum tryptase should be measured at least 24 hours after resolution of anaphylaxis symptoms, even if the acute level was normal.
    Context: Tryptase levels may remain elevated for up to 3 hours; normal levels do not exclude anaphylaxis.
    Rationale: Baseline tryptase helps assess for mast cell disorders and interpret acute increases.
    Source heading: DIAGNOSTIC TESTS IN ACUTE ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_22
    Statement: A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used to diagnose acute mast cell activation, though it cannot detect all anaphylactic reactions.
    Source heading: DIAGNOSTIC TESTS IN ACUTE ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_23
    Statement: Individualized anaphylaxis management plans should be part of long-term care for all patients who have experienced anaphylaxis.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_24
    Statement: At discharge, patients at risk of recurrence should be prescribed self-injectable epinephrine, trained in its use, and provided with a written anaphylaxis emergency action plan and medical identification.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_25
    Statement: Where epinephrine auto-injectors are unavailable or unaffordable, alternative formulations such as prefilled epinephrine syringes (or 1-mL syringe/needle with ampoule) may be recommended, with adequate training and written instructions.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_26
    Statement: Patients with anaphylaxis should be referred to an allergy/immunology specialist for confirmation of triggers, prevention advice, and consideration of allergen immunotherapy.
    Context: Idiopathic anaphylaxis is considered after thorough investigation.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_27
    Statement: Vigilant avoidance of culprit allergens is essential to prevent anaphylaxis recurrence.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_28
    Statement: In medication-induced anaphylaxis, avoidance of the offending drug and use of safe substitutes are mandatory; drug desensitization may be considered if no alternative therapy exists.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_29
    Statement: Annual follow-up is recommended to review recurrence prevention, epinephrine auto-injector technique, and optimize control of comorbidities such as asthma.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  - Rec id: rec_30
    Statement: Follow-up with a dietitian and psychologist may be important, as indicated.
    Source heading: LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_01
  Type: table
  Title: Current definitions of anaphylaxis in the literature
  Source heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Organization: WAO 2011 (1)
      Definition: A serious lifethreatening generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction.
    Row 2:
      Organization: EAACI 2013 (2)
      Definition: A severe lifethreatening generalized or systemic hypersensitivity reaction.
    Row 3:
      Organization: AAAI/ACAAI 2010 (11)
      Definition: An acute, potentially fatal, multi-organ system, allergic reaction.
    Row 4:
      Organization: ASCIA 2016 (16)
      Definition: Any acute onset illness with typical skin features (urticarial rash or erythema/flushing, and/or angioedema), PLUS involvement of respiratory and/or cardiovascular and/ or persistent severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or Any acute onset of hypotension or bronchospasm or upper airway obstruction where anaphylaxis is considered possible, even if typical skin features are not present.
    Row 5:
      Organization: NIAID 2006 (13)
      Definition: Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction that involves more than one organ system (for example, skin, respiratory tract, and/or gastrointestinal tract). It can begin very rapidly, and symptoms may be severe or lifethreatening.
    Row 6:
      Organization: WHO ICD-11 2019
      Definition: Anaphylaxis is a severe, lifethreatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by being rapid in onset with potentially life-threatening airway, breathing, or circulatory problems and is usually, although not always, associated with skin and mucosal changes.
  Summary: This table compiles definitions of anaphylaxis from various allergy organizations, highlighting the common emphasis on severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reactions.
  Clinical relevance: Understanding the different definitions is crucial for consistent diagnosis and management, as some require multi-organ involvement while others focus on specific clinical features.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_02
  Type: table
  Title: Amended criteria for the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
  Source heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Criterion: 1
      Details: Acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with simultaneous involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (eg, generalized hives, pruritus or flushing, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) AND AT LEAST ONE OF THE FOLLOWING: a. Respiratory compromise (eg, dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, reduced PEF, hypoxemia) b. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (eg, hypotonia [collapse], syncope, incontinence) c. Severe gastrointestinal symptoms (eg, severe crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting), especially after exposure to non-food allergens
    Row 2:
      Criterion: 2
      Details: Acute onset of hypotensiona or bronchospasmb or laryngeal involvementc after exposure to a known or highly probable allergend for that patient (minutes to several hours), even in the absence of typical skin involvement.
    Row 3:
      Criterion: Footnotes
      Details: a. Hypotension defined as a decrease in systolic BP greater than 30% from that person's baseline, OR i. Infants and children under 10 years: systolic BP less than (70 mmHg þ [2 x age in years]) ii. Adults and children over 10 years: systolic BP less than <90 mmHg. b. Excluding lower respiratory symptoms triggered by common inhalant allergens or food allergens perceived to cause “inhalational” reactions in the absence of ingestion. c. Laryngeal symptoms include: stridor, vocal changes, odynophagia. d. An allergen is a substance (usually a protein) capable of triggering an immune response that can result in an allergic reaction. Most allergens act through an IgEmediated pathway, but some non-allergen triggers can act independent of IgE (for example, via direct activation of mast cells).
  Summary: This table presents the revised diagnostic criteria developed by the WAO Anaphylaxis Committee, simplifying the previous NIAID/FAAN criteria into two main conditions based on skin involvement and known allergen exposure.
  Clinical relevance: These criteria aim to increase sensitivity in identifying anaphylaxis, especially in presentations without skin signs or cardiovascular shock, to ensure timely and appropriate treatment.

chunks.doc_id: GUIDELINE - Cardona et al. - 2020 - World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_03
  Type: algorithm
  Title: Diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of anaphylaxis
  Source heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
  Description: The figure illustrates two main diagnostic pathways: 1. If there is acute onset with skin or mucosal involvement (e.g., hives, pruritus, angioedema) PLUS respiratory compromise, reduced blood pressure/end-organ dysfunction, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms, then anaphylaxis is highly likely. 2. If the patient has acute onset of hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after exposure to a known or probable allergen, even without skin involvement, anaphylaxis should be considered. The criteria emphasize that typical skin features are not always present.
  Summary: This flowchart depicts the amended WAO diagnostic algorithm, simplifying the previous criteria to aid rapid clinical recognition.
  Clinical relevance: Early recognition using these criteria is critical to initiate prompt treatment with intramuscular epinephrine, reducing the risk of fatal outcomes.

  Source heading: DEFINITION AND CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA FOR ANAPHYLAXIS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Differential diagnoses: Flush syndromes
    Row 2:

    Row 5:

      Differential diagnoses: Autonomic epilepsy

    Row 9:

    Row 18:
      Differential diagnoses: Scombroidosisb
    Row 19:
      Differential diagnoses: Shock

      Differential diagnoses: Pollen-food allergy syndromec
    Row 21:
      Differential diagnoses: Hypovolemic
    Row 22:
      Differential diagnoses: Monosodium glutamate
    Row 23:
      Differential diagnoses: Cardiogenic
    Row 24:
      Differential diagnoses: Sulfites
    Row 25:
      Differential diagnoses: Distributived
    Row 26:
      Differential diagnoses: Food poisoning
    Row 27:
      Differential diagnoses: Septic
    Row 28:
      Differential diagnoses: Excess endogenous histamine
    Row 29:
      Differential diagnoses: Other
    Row 30:
      Differential diagnoses: Mastocytosis/clonal mast cell disorderse
    Row 31:
      Differential diagnoses: Nonallergic angioedema
    Row 32:
      Differential diagnoses: Basophilic leukemia
    Row 33:
      Differential diagnoses: Hereditary angioedema types I, II, & III
    Row 34:
      Differential diagnoses: ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema
    Row 35:
      Differential diagnoses: Systemic capillary leak syndrome
    Row 36:
      Differential diagnoses: Red man syndrome (vancomycin)
    Row 37:
      Differential diagnoses: Pheochromocytoma (paradoxical response)
    Row 38:
      Differential diagnoses: Footnotes: a. Acute asthma symptoms, acute generalized urticaria, or myocardial infarction symptoms can also occur during an anaphylactic episode. b. Histamine poisoning from fish, eg, tuna that has been stored at an elevated temperature; usually, more than one person eating the fish is affected. c. Pollen-food allergy syndrome is elicited by fruits and vegetables containing various plant proteins that cross-react with airborne allergens. Typical symptoms include oral allergy symptoms (itching, tingling and angioedema of the lips, tongue, palate, throat, and ears) after eating raw, but not cooked, fruits and vegetables. d. Distributive shock may be due to anaphylaxis or to spinal cord injury. e. In mastocytosis and clonal mast cell disorders, there is an increased risk of anaphylaxis; also, anaphylaxis may be the first manifestation of the disease.
  Summary: This table lists various conditions that can mimic anaphylaxis, including vasovagal syncope, acute asthma, panic attacks, and other syndromes, emphasizing the need for accurate diagnosis.
  Clinical relevance: Recognizing these mimics is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and ensure appropriate treatment, as some, like acute asthma or myocardial infarction, may coexist with anaphylaxis.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_05
  Type: figure
  Title: Types of anaphylaxis
  Source heading: Pathogenesis of anaphylaxis
  Description: The figure illustrates the different underlying mechanisms of anaphylaxis, including IgE-mediated (classic pathway via allergen-IgE-FcεRI on mast cells/basophils), non-IgE-mediated immunologic (complement, contact/coagulation system, IgG-mediated), and non-immunologic (direct mast cell activation via MRGPRX2, opioids, physical factors). It highlights that multiple pathways may coexist.
  Summary: This figure outlines the pathogenic classifications of anaphylaxis, differentiating between IgE-dependent and IgE-independent triggers.
  Clinical relevance: Understanding the mechanism helps tailor diagnostic testing and management, particularly in identifying idiopathic cases or atypical triggers like alpha-gal.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_08
  Type: table
  Title: Recommended doses for intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
  Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Patient group: Infants under 10 kg
      Dose: 0.01 mg/kg = 0.01 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
    Row 2:
      Patient group: Children aged 1–5 years
      Dose: 0.15 mg = 0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
    Row 3:
      Patient group: Children aged 6–12 years
      Dose: 0.3 mg = 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
    Row 4:
      Patient group: Teenagers and adults
      Dose: 0.5 mg = 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
    Row 5:
      Patient group: Footnote: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) is recommended for intramuscular injections as this allows a more appropriate volume to be injected
  Summary: This table provides age- and weight-based dosing for intramuscular epinephrine, the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
  Clinical relevance: Accurate dosing ensures rapid and effective delivery of epinephrine to reverse severe reactions while minimizing side effects.

      Grade 1: Gastrointestinal
      Grade 2: Upper airway
      Grade 3: Collapse/ hypotension
    Row 5:
      Organ system: Upper respiratory
      Grade 1: Nasal symptoms (eg, sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, and/or nasal congestion)
      Grade 2: Abdominal cramps* and/or vomiting/ diarrhea
      Grade 3: Laryngeal edema with stridor
      Grade 4: And/or

      Grade 1: Uterine cramps
      Grade 2: Any symptom(s) sign(s) from grades 1, 3, or would be included

      Grade 1: Erythema, pruritus, or tearing
      Grade 2: Any symptom(s)/ sign(s) from grade 1 would be included

      Grade 1: Nausea Metallic taste
    Row 10:
      Organ system: Footnotes
      Grade 1: a. Application-site reactions would be considered local reactions. Oral mucosa symptoms, such as pruritus, after sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) administration, or warmth and/or pruritus at a subcutaneous immunotherapy injection site would be considered a local reaction. Gastrointestinal tract reactions after SLIT or oral immunotherapy (OIT) would also be considered local reactions, unless they occur with other systemic manifestations. SLIT or OIT reactions associated with gastrointestinal tract and other systemic manifestations would be classified as SARs.   Summary: This table presents the modified WAO grading system for systemic allergic reactions, categorizing symptoms from one organ system (Grade 1, not anaphylaxis) to life-threatening respiratory/cardiovascular collapse (Grades 4-5, anaphylaxis).
  Clinical relevance: The grading system aids in standardizing severity assessment, identifying reactions that meet anaphylaxis criteria (Grades 3-5) and guiding appropriate treatment intensity.

  Title: Factors and cofactors influencing anaphylaxis
  Source heading: ELICITORS AND COFACTORS OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  Description: The figure depicts the interplay of endogenous (e.g., age, sex, mastocytosis, cardiovascular disease) and exogenous (e.g., exercise, alcohol, medications like beta-blockers/ACE inhibitors) cofactors that can lower the threshold for or increase the severity of an anaphylactic reaction. It stresses that cofactor presence should be assessed in every patient.
  Summary: This illustration highlights how patient-specific and environmental factors can modulate anaphylaxis severity, complementing the list in Table 5.
  Clinical relevance: Identifying and mitigating cofactors is key to preventing severe recurrences, as these modifiable factors may be avoidable.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_11
  Type: flowchart
  Title: Management of anaphylaxis
  Source heading: ACUTE TREATMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS
  Description: The flowchart outlines the acute management steps: 1. Remove the trigger if possible. 2. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin. 3. Call for emergency services. 4. Administer intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh. 5. Position the patient supine (or semi-recumbent on left if pregnant, recovery position if unconscious). 6. Upon healthcare arrival, provide high-flow oxygen, establish IV access, give IV fluid bolus for cardiovascular instability, and consider cardiopulmonary resuscitation if needed. 7. For bronchoconstriction, inhaled beta-2 agonists may be given, but epinephrine remains primary. 8. Second-line medications (antihistamines, glucocorticoids) may be considered. 9. Monitor and repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. 10. Observe for at least 6-12 hours due to risk of biphasic reaction.
  Summary: This algorithm presents a stepwise emergency response for anaphylaxis, emphasizing early intramuscular epinephrine as the cornerstone of treatment.
  Clinical relevance: Following this standardized approach reduces mortality and ensures timely intervention, especially in settings where healthcare professionals may be hesitant to use epinephrine.
